title: A birthday and a promise

facts.text: The Tehran Conference ran from 28 November to 1 December 1943 at the Soviet Embassy in Tehran. It brought Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin together at the same table.
Stalin had pressed his Western allies for a second front in Europe since 1941.

On the morning of 30 November 1943 the British and American chiefs agreed to recommend that Stalin be told the Anglo-American forces would launch Overlord during the month of May, together with a supporting operation against the south of France.

Before lunch on 30 November, at Churchill's request, Roosevelt read Stalin the recommendations of the combined British and American staffs. Stalin expressed his great satisfaction and said the Red Army would undertake offensive operations at the same time.

At the 4 p.m. session that day Stalin said the Soviets would organize a large scale offensive against the Germans in May, to hold the most German divisions on the Eastern Front and stop them moving west against Overlord.

30 November 1943 was Churchill's 69th birthday. That evening 33 members of the American, British and Soviet delegations gathered with him for dinner. Roosevelt sat on his right and Stalin on his left.
Every speech took the form of a toast. Churchill toasted Stalin as worthy to stand with the great figures of Russian history, meriting the title Stalin the Great.

Stalin asked for one more toast at the end. He praised American production, said he had been told the United States would soon build 10,000 planes a month against the Soviet Union's 2,500 to 3,000, and said with emphasis that without the planes from America the war would have been lost.
Overlord, the Normandy landings, began on 6 June 1944. The Soviet summer offensive the Allies had been promised, Operation Bagration, followed later that month.
The photo shows Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill seated on the portico of the Soviet Embassy in Tehran during the conference. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, National Archives 342-FH-3A48363.

U.S. Army Signal Corps reel 111-ADC-1015 shows the conference grounds: a Soviet guard of honor marching past the Soviet Embassy portico, the Soviet emblem on the embassy, British delegates in the British Embassy garden, and Stalin among the delegates outside. It is silent.

declassified.fact: At the birthday dinner Stalin teased Gen. Sir Alan Brooke for being unfriendly to the Soviets. When Brooke answered that Stalin might have mistaken British dummy tanks and planes for the real thing, Stalin cut in dryly, "That is possible," and when Brooke said he wanted closer collaboration, "That is possible, even probable."

video.hook: His last toast was to American factories.

body:
On his 69th birthday, Winston Churchill sat at dinner between the two men he needed most. That same day, Stalin finally got the promise he had pressed for since 1941.

30 November 1943, Tehran. Before lunch Roosevelt read Stalin the Allied chiefs' decision: the invasion of France, Operation Overlord, would come in May 1944. Stalin said he was greatly satisfied, and pledged a Red Army offensive at the same time.

That night 33 guests filled Churchill's table, with Roosevelt on his right and Stalin on his left. Churchill toasted "Stalin the Great." The final toast was Stalin's own, and it went to American factories: without the planes from America, he said, the war would have been lost.

On his 69th birthday, Churchill sat at dinner between Roosevelt and Stalin.

30 November 1943, Tehran. That day Stalin was told the invasion of France would come in May 1944, and he pledged a Red Army offensive to match. His last toast of the night went to American factories: without their planes, he said, the war would have been lost.
